# Event Logging Under the GCC-Moderate FedRAMP Boundary — What's Blocked, Why, and the Limits of Recovery {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**[Download this whitepaper as DOCX](event-logging-fedramp-boundary-limitations.docx)** — a Word copy of
this page, regenerated on every site deploy. (Also available from the
**Other Formats** link in the page sidebar.)
:::
:::

## The problem this paper resolves

Two very different pieces of Microsoft technology sit underneath the same
question an agency operating M365 GCC-Moderate under a FedRAMP Moderate
authorization has to answer: *what am I actually able to see, and what have
I quietly lost?*

**Windows Event Viewer** is the decades-old, on-endpoint audit log — the
System, Security, Application, and role-specific channels every Windows
device already writes to, and the substrate NIST SP 800-53's audit family
(AU-2, AU-3, AU-12) and OMB M-21-31's event-logging maturity tiers are
written about. **Azure Event Hubs** is the opposite end of the pipe: a
tenant-scale, PaaS streaming broker an agency can stand up *inside its own
authorization boundary* to land diagnostic and audit exports at scale — the
mechanism the in-boundary rebuild plan in
[B.1.3](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd)
depends on.

Neither tool is itself blocked by the FedRAMP Moderate boundary. What *is*
blocked is a specific, enumerated set of 26 telemetry signals — mostly
Microsoft's own cloud-side computed products (risk scores, adoption
aggregates, ML-driven anomaly detections) built **on top of** raw data that
Event Viewer and equivalent cloud audit logs already produce. This paper is
the full accounting: which signals are blocked, why, what actually breaks
as a result, and how far an Event Hub-based in-boundary pipeline can
recover them. **Scope:** this paper draws every fact from the 26-row gap
matrix and the B.1/B.1.1/B.1.3 boundary-model leaves; where this page and
those leaves disagree, the leaves are authoritative — see [Honest limits
and scope](#honest-limits-and-scope).

## Executive summary

- **26 telemetry signals are documented as blocked, restricted, or
  retention-limited** under the GCC-Moderate FedRAMP Moderate authorization
  boundary — confirmed by Microsoft documentation for some, inferred from
  the boundary's own SI-4/AU-2/AU-3/SC-7 architecture for most.
- **The constraint is the destination, not the data.** Raw telemetry —
  including the Windows Event Viewer-sourced records behind the Endpoint
  Analytics family — is collectible in-boundary. What GCC-Moderate does not
  provision is Microsoft's **commercial multi-tenant ML and analytics
  layer** built on top of that raw data. An agency can land the same raw
  records in its own Event Hub → SIEM pipeline and rebuild an approximation
  of the missing layer, *inside* its own boundary.
- **Of the 26 signals: 8 are fully rebuildable, 16 partially, 2 not at
  all.** The two irreducible losses are structural, not a resourcing
  problem: cross-tenant access telemetry (the agency never holds the other
  tenant's data) and Office "Optional" diagnostic data (suppressed at the
  client before collection, not merely unexported).
- **Ramifications land hardest on four fronts:** Zero Trust risk scoring
  loses its fastest, most-tuned inputs (Entra risk detection degrades from
  commercial minutes to GCC-Moderate hours-to-days); anomaly detection loses
  what the source data itself calls an "infinite gap" for network-path
  attacks (BGP hijack, DNS manipulation, MITM are natively undetectable);
  insider-risk signals — digital disengagement, DLP override patterns, data
  hoarding — degrade or disappear; and forensic reconstruction hits a hard
  28-day wall on location telemetry unless an agency exports before the
  purge.
- **Full compensation is not achievable at any investment level.** The
  rebuild reaches functional coverage and Advanced ZTMM maturity on most
  pillars; it does not reach commercial fidelity or Optimal maturity on any
  pillar, and two specific losses have no rebuild path at all.

## 1. Two tools, two roles

### 1.1 Windows Event Viewer — the on-endpoint audit substrate

Windows Event Viewer (`eventvwr.msc`) is the built-in log reader for the
Windows Event Log service — the System, Security, Application, Setup, and
Forwarded Events channels every Windows endpoint writes to natively, plus
any application- or service-specific channel a piece of software registers
for itself. It is not a Microsoft cloud product; it predates GCC-Moderate,
Entra ID, and Azure entirely, and it keeps writing regardless of tenant,
licensing, or authorization boundary. A concrete example already in this
repository: [`Install-UIAOService.ps1`](../../../deploy/windows-server/Install-UIAOService.ps1)
registers the UIAO Windows service's own Event Viewer log source on
install, exactly the pattern any Windows-hosted federal service uses to
make its own operational and security events auditable.

**Why it matters to a federal agency specifically:** Event Viewer's
Security log is the literal implementation surface for NIST SP 800-53's
audit-family controls — AU-2 (auditable events), AU-3 (content of audit
records), AU-12 (audit generation) — at the endpoint. OMB M-21-31 (event
logging maturity tiers EL0 through EL3) is a federal mandate specifically
about centralizing, retaining, and protecting exactly this class of log;
[Federal Compliance for Moderate
Agencies](federal-compliance-for-moderate-agencies.qmd) names M-21-31 as
real and agency-facing but out of scope for that primer on length grounds —
this paper is where it becomes directly relevant, because Event Viewer logs
are the input M-21-31 governs the handling of.

**Its role in the gap matrix:** Microsoft's Endpoint Analytics – Advanced
service does not invent new data — it reads System/Application-channel
events and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) providers already on the device
(boot-phase timings, application crash/hang records, stop-error/bugcheck
events, resource-usage counters), rolls them up through the Intune/Defender
agent, and computes trend and anomaly products on Microsoft's commercial
cloud side. **That rollup-and-compute layer is what GCC-Moderate does not
provision** — not the underlying Event Viewer data, which the endpoint
keeps writing either way.

### 1.2 Azure Event Hubs — the in-boundary rebuild transport

Azure Event Hubs is a PaaS, tenant-scale streaming/ingestion broker — the
Azure equivalent of a partitioned commit log, built to absorb diagnostic
and audit exports at volumes a single-endpoint tool like Event Viewer was
never meant to handle. It runs in Azure Commercial and inherits Azure's own
FedRAMP Moderate/High P-ATO, so it does not require a separate
authorization to use inside a GCC-Moderate boundary. Because it is PaaS,
**the agency owns the data plane**: its own namespace, its own retention,
its own network path (Private Link / disabled public access), its own
encryption keys if required. That is precisely the property that keeps it
out of the blocked category the rest of this paper describes — it is not a
Microsoft-operated multi-tenant analytics service the boundary is built to
keep raw telemetry away from; it is agency-operated transport the boundary
was drawn to *permit*.

**Its role in the rebuild:** nearly every Azure, Entra, and M365-adjacent
resource that emits diagnostic or audit data can stream it to an Event Hub
namespace via Diagnostic Settings. Downstream, an in-boundary SIEM
(Sentinel, Log Analytics, or a third-party equivalent — see [B.1.3
§9](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd#9-authorization-compliance-hygiene)
on keeping every hop in-boundary) subscribes and lands the data. Event Hubs
is Layer 1 (**Collection**) of the five-layer in-boundary rebuild
architecture B.1.3 specifies in full — see that leaf for the complete
implementation plan; this paper does not re-derive it.

### 1.3 How they connect — and where they don't

The two tools are not one continuous pipe for every blocked signal. They
connect only for the subset of the gap matrix that actually originates as
an on-endpoint Windows Event Viewer / ETW record:

| Signal family | Originates in Event Viewer/ETW? | Rebuild transport |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint Analytics – Advanced (6 rows: boot performance, crash/hang rate, CPU/memory, stop-error restarts, battery/WFA, performance regression) | **Yes** — System/Application channel events and ETW counters, rolled up by the Intune/Defender agent | Defender `DeviceEvents` / Graph device export → Event Hub → in-boundary Log Analytics → agency anomaly model |
| Adoption Score, Entra ID, Intune behavioral, M365 core/Purview, Microsoft INR, Teams CQD (20 rows) | **No** — these originate as service-side audit/diagnostic records in Microsoft's cloud, not on the endpoint | Entra/Intune/Purview Diagnostic Settings → Event Hub → in-boundary Log Analytics directly; Event Viewer is not in this chain at all |

This distinction matters for accuracy: Event Viewer explains *why* the
Endpoint Analytics family is rebuildable at all (the raw data already
exists locally, in-boundary, and always did). It says nothing about the
other twenty signals — those are blocked or restricted for reasons internal
to Microsoft's cloud-side collection decisions, covered next.

## 2. Where and why the boundary blocks telemetry

The full architectural argument is [B.1's boundary
model](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-gcc-moderate-boundary-model.qmd) and
[B.1.3 §2's in-boundary
principle](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd#2-the-in-boundary-principle-why-this-is-lawful-where-inheritance-is-not);
the load-bearing fact, restated for this paper's purpose:

**The FedRAMP Moderate authorization boundary constrains where
identity-attributed, behavioral telemetry may go — not whether an agency
may collect and analyze it at all.** SI-4 (system monitoring), AU-2/AU-3
(audit events and content), and SC-7 (boundary protection) govern the
*export destination*. Sending that data to Microsoft's commercial
multi-tenant machine-learning and analytics services is the flow the
boundary restricts, because that destination sits outside the agency's own
authorization scope. Sending the same data to an agency-owned, in-boundary
SIEM is not restricted — it is exactly the in-boundary monitoring SI-4 and
AU-2/AU-3 contemplate.

That single distinction produces every row in the gap matrix, but through
three different mechanisms (`documented` status in the underlying
[`gcc-moderate-telemetry-gaps.yaml`](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/data/gcc-moderate-telemetry-gaps.yaml)):

| Mechanism | What it means | How many of the 26 rows |
|---|---|---|
| **Confirmed** | Microsoft documentation explicitly states the product/feature is unavailable in GCC-Moderate | 8 |
| **Inferred** | No explicit Microsoft statement; blocked as a consequence of the SI-4/AU-2/AU-3/SC-7 boundary architecture itself | 15 |
| **Restricted** | Available, but defaulted off or scoped down (e.g., Office "Optional" diagnostic data defaults to the narrower "Required" tier) | 1 |
| **Retention-limited** | Available, but a shortened data-lifetime cap creates a forensic cliff before an agency can act on or export it | 2 |

The **why** varies by row, but resolves to one of three underlying causes,
each with a different rebuild prognosis (full detail in [B.1.3
§3](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd#3-scope-what-can-and-cannot-be-rebuilt)):

1. **Only the ML/analytics layer is missing; raw telemetry is collectible
   in-boundary** — fully the agency's to rebuild (this is the Event
   Viewer-sourced Endpoint Analytics family, and most of the Entra/Intune
   behavioral rows).
2. **Microsoft's specific computed product's inputs never reach the
   tenant** — a different in-boundary source can substitute, but the exact
   Microsoft product cannot be recreated (Adoption Score, INR).
3. **The data itself is never the agency's to hold, or never collected at
   all** — irreducible; no rebuild closes it (cross-tenant telemetry,
   suppressed-at-source Office diagnostics).

| Content collaboration (attachments vs. cloud links) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Data, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute |
| Mobility (multi-platform usage patterns) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Identity, Devices | Partial — substitute |

| Apps Health (update channel, version telemetry) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Applications & Workloads, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute |
| Network connectivity scores (per location) | SI-4, SC-7 | Networks, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute |
| Endpoint readiness baselines (tenant-wide) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute |

| Signal | Constraining controls | ZTMM pillar(s) | Rebuild verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| INR real-time path metrics (latency / jitter / packet-loss) | SC-7 | Networks, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute (agency-owned PEP telemetry, not Microsoft path intelligence) |

|---|---|---|---|

| App reliability (crash count, hang rate, stability) | SI-4, SC-7 | Devices, Applications & Workloads | Partial — substitute |
| Resource performance (CPU / memory spikes) | SI-4, SC-7 | Devices | Partial — substitute (high value — recovers grey-ware/miner/exfil signal) |
| Stop-error restarts | SI-4, SC-7 | Devices, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute |
| Battery health / work-from-anywhere readiness | SI-4, SC-7 | Devices | Partial — substitute (low value) |
| Device performance anomalies (post-config / policy / OS regression) | SI-4, SC-7 | Devices, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute |

### 3.4 Entra ID (3 signals — inferred)

| Signal | Constraining controls | ZTMM pillar(s) | Rebuild verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Real-time risk scores / Identity Protection ML | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3, SC-7 | Identity, Visibility & Analytics | **Fixes** (minutes-to-hours, not commercial minutes; no global threat intel) |
| Cross-tenant access telemetry (B2B, Direct Connect) | SI-4, SC-7 | Identity | **Not fixed** — irreducible |
| Real-time CAE revocation paths (sub-second) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3, SC-7 | Identity, Automation & Orchestration | Partial — bounded (minutes via SOAR, not sub-second) |

### 3.5 Intune (3 signals — inferred)

| Signal | Constraining controls | ZTMM pillar(s) | Rebuild verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| App-protection policy violation analytics | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Devices, Applications & Workloads | **Fixes** (snapshot-driven, not real-time behavioral) |
| WUfB deployment health trends / per-device error codes | SI-4, SC-7 | Devices, Visibility & Analytics | **Fixes** (reporting lag vs. Microsoft real-time) |
| EPM elevation operational analytics (process metadata) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Devices, Identity, Visibility & Analytics | **Fixes** (conditional on elevation-event collectibility) |

### 3.6 M365 core / Purview (4 signals — restricted or inferred)

| Signal | Constraining controls | ZTMM pillar(s) | Rebuild verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Office "Optional" diagnostic data | SI-4 | Applications & Workloads, Devices | **Not fixed** — suppressed at source |
| Copilot / AI prompt-response telemetry richness | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Applications & Workloads, Visibility & Analytics | Partial — substitute (incident counts only) |
| Sensitivity-label usage analytics | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Data, Visibility & Analytics | **Fixes** |
| DLP behavioral richness (override, near-miss, fingerprint context) | SI-4, AU-2, AU-3 | Data, Visibility & Analytics | **Fixes** (pattern rules only, no content-fingerprint model) |

### 3.7 Teams CQD (2 signals — retention-limited)

| Signal | Constraining controls | ZTMM pillar(s) | Rebuild verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long-term EUII (BSSID, public IP, subnet/building) — 28-day retention | SI-4 | Networks | **Fixes** (retention fix — export before purge) |
| Cross-product 12+ month historical pivots | SI-4 | Visibility & Analytics | **Fixes** (agency long-retention store) |

**Coverage total:** 8 fixes, 16 partial (substitute or bounded), 2 not
fixed — the complete row-by-row verdict, with residual notes for every row,
is [B.1.3
§6.1](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd#61-complete-fix-coverage-matrix-all-26-gap-rows).

## 4. Full ramifications, by impact dimension

Each blocked signal in the source yaml carries claims across four
dimensions. Grouped thematically rather than row-by-row, the ramifications
are:

### 4.1 Zero Trust — weaker inputs to every access decision

Nearly every blocked signal removes a behavioral baseline Conditional
Access and risk-based policy would otherwise consume. The sharpest,
quantified instance: Entra Identity Protection's real-time risk detection
— the single highest-value rebuildable signal in the matrix — degrades from
**commercial-cloud minutes to GCC-Moderate hours-to-days** without an
agency-built rebuild. Elsewhere the loss is qualitative but still concrete:
no "expected communication behavior" baseline for identity verification, no
path-aware trust for network access (INR), reduced confidence in
remote-endpoint trust (battery/WFA), and — for real-time session revocation
(CAE) — a token-theft exposure window that widens from under 15 minutes
commercial to 60–90 minutes even after the SOAR-based rebuild in §5.

### 4.2 Anomaly detection — some losses are total, not partial

Most rows describe a *degraded* anomaly-detection capability; one is
described in the source data as an outright **"infinite gap"**: without INR
real-time path metrics, an agency has no native ability to detect BGP
hijack, DNS manipulation, or man-in-the-middle path attacks at all — a
substitute (SD-WAN/SASE path telemetry, per ADR-057) is available, but the
underlying Microsoft signal cannot be reconstructed. Resource-performance
telemetry loss is flagged similarly severe: hidden cryptocurrency miners or
exfiltration tooling that bypasses antivirus can go unnoticed without
CPU/memory anomaly detection. WUfB's rebuilt patch-posture view still lags
Microsoft's real-time fleet view by 7–14 days.

### 4.3 Insider risk — several signals are named explicitly as flight-risk or exfiltration indicators

The communication-pattern loss (chat vs. email) is flagged **Critical** in
the source data specifically for losing the "digital-disengagement /
flight-risk" signal — a leading indicator security teams use ahead of
insider incidents. Content-collaboration loss (attachments vs. cloud links)
is flagged **High** for the same reason in reverse: users regressing to
local copies to route around DLP becomes invisible. DLP behavioral richness
loss removes override-pattern insider signal entirely absent the rebuild.
On the endpoint side, CAE's bounded rebuild means a compromised or
insider-abused session can persist up to 90 minutes before an automated
revocation fires, versus near-instant commercial containment.

### 4.4 Forensics — two hard limits, not gradual degradation

Two items in this dimension are not "reduced visibility" but genuine
cliffs. First, Teams CQD's 28-day EUII retention window is flagged as a
**critical forensic cliff** — location/network forensic detail (BSSID,
public IP, subnet/building) is gone permanently after 28 days unless an
agency schedules export before the purge; incident response that starts
more than four weeks after the fact has nothing to reconstruct from. Second,
Office "Optional" diagnostic data's client-side telemetry — the
"contextual glue" between Office and Teams app navigation used to
reconstruct lateral movement — is **suppressed at the client before
collection**, meaning no forensic rebuild is possible at any budget; it was
never captured to begin with. Cross-tenant B2B/Direct Connect timeline
reconstruction is similarly capped: the agency's own audit logs show its
side of the interaction, never the counterpart tenant's.

## 5. What the Event Hub-based rebuild recovers — and what it cannot

Per [B.1.3](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd),
the rebuild is a five-layer, Event Hub-anchored architecture: **Collection**
(Diagnostic Settings and Graph exports landing in an in-boundary Event Hub
namespace) → **Store** (a durable, retention-correct Log Analytics
workspace) → **Analytics & ML** (KQL detection rules and, where budget and
authorization allow, trained models) → **Response** (SOAR playbooks that
approximate the automated containment Microsoft's SaaS layer provided) →
**Policy feedback** (the rebuilt risk signal wired back into Conditional
Access). That full implementation plan — phased, with effort bands, cost
and staffing realities, and detection-engineering patterns — is out of
scope for this paper; see B.1.3 in full.

What this paper adds is the honest ceiling on that effort: **the rebuild
recovers functional coverage, not commercial fidelity.** Of the 26 signals,
8 reach full functional parity (mostly retention fixes and rule-based
reconstructions of Microsoft's ML layer), 16 land as agency-owned
substitutes that answer the same security question at reduced fidelity or
latency, and 2 — cross-tenant access telemetry and Office "Optional"
diagnostic data — have no rebuild path at any investment level, for reasons
that are structural (the agency never holds the other tenant's data; the
client never collected the data to begin with), not budgetary.

## 6. Honest limits and scope {#honest-limits-and-scope}

- **This paper is a synthesis, not a primary source.** Every fact above is
  already established, in more depth, by
  [`gcc-moderate-telemetry-gaps.yaml`](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/data/gcc-moderate-telemetry-gaps.yaml)
  and the [B.1](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-gcc-moderate-boundary-model.qmd) /
  [B.1.1](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-1-gcc-moderate-three-way-conflict.qmd) /
  [B.1.3](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd)
  leaves. Where this page and those sources disagree, the yaml and the
  leaves are authoritative — this page should be corrected to match them,
  not the reverse.
- **Full compensation is not achievable.** Per [B.1.3
  §11](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd#11-compensation-ceiling-can-the-telemetry-location-blocks-be-fully-compensated),
  the rebuild reaches functional parity for most signals and Advanced ZTMM
  maturity on most pillars, but not fidelity parity on ML-driven signals
  and not Optimal maturity on any pillar. This paper does not repeat that
  leaf's full diminishing-returns analysis; it is the authority on the
  question.
- **Windows Event Viewer explains one family of six rows, not all
  twenty-six.** §1.3's table is explicit about which signals trace to
  on-endpoint Event Viewer/ETW data and which are cloud-native audit
  records with no Event Viewer involvement at all — treating this paper's
  title as implying Event Viewer is the source of every blocked signal
  would overstate its role.
- **Location telemetry carries additional, non-technical ceilings** — the
  E911 dispatchable-location statutory obligation and EO 14117's
  regulatory handling restrictions — that no telemetry rebuild touches.
  This paper covers only the telemetry dimension; see [B.1.3
  §11.3](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd#113-location-blocks-a-harder-ceiling-than-telemetry-in-general)
  for the fuller location-specific analysis.
- **Scope is federal civilian, GCC-Moderate baseline.** DoD environments
  (IL4/IL5, GCC High) and non-federal compliance regimes are out of scope;
  several products named above have GCC-High-specific availability that
  differs from what is documented here.
- **This is not legal or compliance advice**, and the gap matrix's
  `documented` status for `inferred` rows is an architectural inference
  from SI-4/AU-2/AU-3/SC-7, not a Microsoft-published statement — verify
  current availability directly against Microsoft's GCC-Moderate service
  descriptions before treating any specific row as load-bearing for an ATO
  package.

## Call to Action

::: {.callout-important}
## Three steps to start this quarter

1. **Inventory which of the 26 rows your agency actually depends on today.**
   Cross-reference §3's grouped tables against the dashboards your SOC and
   IT operations teams already use — Adoption Score, Endpoint Analytics,
   Entra ID risk scoring, Intune, Purview, Teams CQD — and flag the rows
   your incident-response or insider-risk program has silently assumed are
   still working.
2. **Close the two retention cliffs first — they are the cheapest fixes in
   the matrix.** Scheduling CQD export before the 28-day EUII purge and
   standing up a long-retention store for 12+ month historical pivots are
   both fully rebuildable at low cost, per §3.7, with no ML or SOAR
   investment required.
3. **Read [B.1.3](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-3-rebuilding-boundary-blocked-analytics.qmd)
   in full before scoping an Event Hub-based rebuild program.** This paper
   established what is blocked and why; B.1.3 is the phased implementation
   plan, cost model, and detection-engineering patterns for actually
   building the Layer 1–5 stack this paper describes only at the
   architecture level.
:::
